name: Leanmaxxing via bloodletting

card.summary: A fringe forum idea that deliberately losing blood forces the body to spend extra calories regrowing it, supposedly speeding fat loss for a leaner look.
card.note: Blood loss carries risks of anemia, infection and shock; clinical phlebotomy is a supervised treatment for specific conditions, not a weight-loss method.

quick.overview:
Leanmaxxing via bloodletting is a fringe theory from a looksmax.org thread. Its author argues that the more resources the body must spend regrowing blood, skin and hair, the more calories it burns, so removing blood would accelerate fat loss and produce a leaner face and body faster than diet and exercise alone.

No published research tests this idea. Bloodletting itself has a long medical history and a small number of modern supervised uses, such as treating iron overload, and the medical literature documents its harms when used excessively.
quick.how: This article does not describe methods. The theory is presented in the thread as an add-on to fasting and training, with the poster claiming large weekly weight loss.
quick.risks: Medical sources describe significant blood loss, anemia, infection, hematoma and, in extreme cases, fatal hypovolemic shock as risks of bloodletting. Weight lost this way is not the same as fat lost. Anyone considering any blood removal is directed by clinicians to supervised settings such as blood donation services or treatment for a diagnosed condition.

lead: Leanmaxxing via bloodletting is a fringe weight-loss idea posted on looksmax.org in a thread titled 'Hardcore Leanmaxxing (Bloodletting Method)'. Its author argues that a body forced to rebuild lost blood, skin and hair spends extra energy, so deliberately removing blood would speed fat loss beyond what training and fasting achieve, producing a leaner face and body sooner. The thread claims an extra 3 to 10 pounds lost per week when combined with cardio, calisthenics and fasting.[1]

The appearance goal is leanness: lower body fat makes the jaw, cheekbones and facial structure more visible, which is the reason 'leanmaxxing' threads are a staple of looksmaxxing forums. The bloodletting thread presents the method as a way to reach that point faster. It is a single-thread idea rather than a movement, and it has no named originator, books or influencer following beyond that post.[1]

Bloodletting itself is an old medical practice. It rested on humoral theory, was central to 18th and 19th century 'heroic medicine', and declined after William Harvey's work on circulation (1628) and Pierre Louis's statistical studies in the 1830s.[2] Today a supervised, small-scale descendant survives as therapeutic phlebotomy for conditions such as hemochromatosis and polycythemia vera, alongside medicinal leech use in some surgical settings.[2][3][6] No published study has tested bloodletting as a method of losing fat, and trials of therapeutic phlebotomy in clinical populations report outcomes unrelated to leanness.[4][5]

chain: Body spends calories replacing it (the theory's premise)
angle.text: The claim is that blood replacement is metabolically costly and so speeds fat loss, helping someone get lean faster. The thread's author describes it as a supplement to fasting and training.

paras: The thread's author says the number one way to lose weight is to keep metabolism 'working overtime', that training and fasting are necessary, and that regrowing things raises calorie consumption, so removing blood accelerates loss. The post states that the body signals when too much has been lost and that water and vitamins let a person rebuild what was lost quickly.[1]
A reply asking how the poster came up with the theory was answered with the statement that it is 'legit'.[1] The thread does not cite medical literature, and the wiki does not reproduce its methods.

The underlying premise echoes a widely repeated figure in popular health writing that replacing a pint of blood costs the body roughly 600 to 650 kilocalories. Science Focus notes that the figure is attributed to the Red Cross and the Mayo Clinic but that the organisations do not give a source for it, and Medical News Today reports that claims of a calorie-burning effect from donation are not supported by scientific evidence and that any calorie loss would be short-term.[8][9]

Bloodletting is the deliberate removal of blood to prevent or treat illness. Under humoral theory, health required balance among bodily fluids; Galen devised a detailed system setting how much blood to remove by age, season and disease. Hippocrates mostly favoured diet, medieval texts tied bleeding sites to astrology, and printed manuals such as Hans von Gersdorff's 1517 book standardised bleeding points.[2]

In the 18th century it became central to heroic medicine, and in the 1800s it was used for nearly every ailment, often performed by barber-surgeons, with leech imports reaching about 40 million a year in France in the 1830s. George Washington died in 1799 after roughly 3.75 litres of blood was removed in ten hours during treatment for a throat infection.[2]

Harvey's circulation work undermined its theory, and Pierre Louis's 1830s statistics showed it ineffective for pneumonia and fevers. Some prominent physicians, including William Osler, still defended it in the 1880s, and a 1923 edition of a major textbook still recommended it.[2]

Therapeutic phlebotomy treats conditions in which red cells or iron must be reduced, notably hemochromatosis, polycythemia vera and porphyria cutanea tarda. The average adult therapeutic draw is about one unit (450 to 500 mL) of whole blood, scheduled weekly to every several months as the clinician decides.[6] Medicinal leeches are used after digital replantation and revascularisation to relieve venous congestion.[3]

Blood donation is a related but distinct activity. The World Health Organization defines a unit as 450 mL, plasma is replaced within about two to three days, and red cells recover more slowly, about 36 days on average in healthy adult men, which is why US donation centres set a 56-day interval between whole-blood donations.[7]
No studies found on bloodletting for fat loss or appearance. Phlebotomy has been studied in other clinical populations.

A 2022 randomised trial in 53 adults with unmedicated grade 1 hypertension compared two 500 mL phlebotomies six weeks apart with a waiting list. The 24-hour mean arterial pressure fell by 1.12 mmHg in the phlebotomy group and rose by 0.43 mmHg in controls, a difference of 1.55 mmHg that was not statistically significant; two adverse events, anaemia and dizziness, were attributed to phlebotomy.[4]

A 2017 randomised study of 274 non-diabetic adults with dysmetabolic iron overload syndrome compared one year of venesections plus lifestyle advice with advice alone. Body weight rose 0.5 percent in the venesection group and fell 0.6 percent in controls, fasting glycaemia did not differ, insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) was higher with venesection, and fatigue occurred in 25.3 percent of venesected patients versus 2.3 percent of controls. The authors concluded that iron depletion did not improve metabolic and hepatic features and that diet and lifestyle remain first-line.[5]

Reference sources describe significant blood loss, anaemia, shock, infection or sepsis and hematoma as harms of bloodletting.[2] For blood donation, the commonest problems are bruising and fainting, with about 2 percent of donors reporting an adverse reaction in one study, and first-time donors, teenagers and women at higher risk.[7] Medical News Today lists weakness, dizziness, nausea and, rarely, convulsions, with younger donors and people of low body weight more likely to be affected.[9]

The forum thread's statement that the body will signal when too much has been lost differs from medical descriptions of hypovolemic shock and from the donation-centre practice of setting minimum weights and hemoglobin thresholds, which in the US Red Cross are 12.5 g/dL for females and 13.0 g/dL for males.[1][2][7] Anyone considering any blood removal is directed by clinicians to supervised settings such as donation services or treatment for a diagnosed condition.

The idea appears in one looksmax.org thread and was presented as an add-on to fasting, cardio and calisthenics in a leanmaxxing routine. Looksmaxxing communities more broadly discuss leanness through diet, training and body-fat reduction, but no widely followed influencer or protocol has adopted bloodletting.[1]

timeline.event: Bloodletting appears in Greek medicine; Hippocrates mostly favours diet while others support the practice.[2]
Hans von Gersdorff's printed surgical manual standardises bleeding points.[2]
William Harvey's work on circulation undermines the theoretical basis of bloodletting.[2]
George Washington dies after about 3.75 litres of blood is removed over ten hours.[2]
Pierre Louis uses statistics to show bloodletting ineffective for pneumonia and fevers; France imports about 40 million leeches a year.[2]
A major medical textbook edition still recommends bloodletting.[2]
A 274-patient randomised study reports no metabolic improvement and higher fatigue with venesection in dysmetabolic iron overload.[5]
A randomised trial of therapeutic phlebotomy in grade 1 hypertension reports a non-significant blood pressure change.[4]

lore.intro: The idea appears in a single looksmax.org thread presenting bloodletting as an advanced leanmaxxing add-on.[1]

claims.claim: Losing blood makes the body burn extra calories regrowing it, so fat loss speeds up.
claims.believers: The thread's author says replacing blood, skin and hair consumes resources and calories, and claims several extra pounds lost per week when combined with working out and fasting.[1]
claims.experts: No published study tests bloodletting as a weight-loss method. A frequently quoted 600 to 650 kilocalorie figure for replacing a pint is attributed to health organisations without a stated source, and a health-news outlet reports no scientific support for a weight-loss effect.[8][9]

claims.claim: The body signals when too much blood has been lost, so the method can be self-regulated.
claims.believers: The thread says a person will know when they have lost too much and can rebuild with water and vitamins.[1]
claims.experts: Medical references list shock, anaemia, infection and hematoma among harms of bloodletting, and donation centres use weight and hemoglobin thresholds.[2][7]

claims.claim: Weight lost this way is leanness gained.
claims.believers: The thread frames the practice as a route to a leaner face and body.[1]
claims.experts: In a randomised study of venesection in iron overload, body weight rose slightly in the venesection group versus a small loss with lifestyle advice alone, and fatigue was more common.[5]

claims.claim: Bloodletting has proven medical benefits that carry over to cosmetic goals.
claims.believers: Supporters point to its long history and continued medical use.[1]
claims.experts: Modern uses are specific: hemochromatosis, polycythemia vera, porphyria cutanea tarda, and leeches after replantation. A hypertension trial found a non-significant blood-pressure change.[3][4][6]
